summaries.example: Imagine seeing a red apple. Your senses give you a direct, particular awareness of this apple. Your thinking can then use ideas such as “apple,” “red,” and “fruit” to organize what you see. Philosophers disagree about whether thinking must already help create the first awareness, or whether the senses can provide it on their own.
summaries.summary: This entry explains a debate about how sensing and thinking work together in Kant’s philosophy. Kant separates sensibility, which receives information, from the intellect, which actively combines and organizes representations. He calls a direct awareness of a particular object an intuition and a general way of thinking about things a concept. The central question is whether intuition can be produced without the intellect. Intellectualists say that some intellectual ability, perhaps the power to bring representations into one conscious unity, is needed. Sensibilists say that at least some intuitions can be generated by sensibility alone. The entry also explains why the usual question—whether experience has conceptual content—may not fit Kant perfectly. It may be better to ask what mental abilities intuition depends on. This matters because the answer affects how we understand perception, knowledge, animals’ mental lives, imagination, mathematics, and Kant’s argument about the categories.
key_ideas: Kant says the mind has different abilities. The senses receive information, while the intellect actively organizes it.
He distinguishes an intuition, which is direct and particular, from a concept, which is general and works through thought.
The debate asks whether an intuition can happen without help from the intellect.
One group, called Intellectualists, says intuition depends at least partly on thinking abilities. Another group, called Sensibilists, says some intuitions can arise independently of the intellect.
Kant’s words “intuition,” “perception,” and “experience” have special meanings, so they should not always be treated as ordinary everyday words.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate helps us ask how seeing and thinking connect. It also asks how sense experience could give us reasons for beliefs instead of merely causing them. Understanding the disagreement can make us more careful when we say that we “see” something, “know” something, or “understand” something.

important_terms.definition: The mind’s ability to receive information through the senses, such as seeing, hearing, or touching.
A direct awareness of one particular thing, such as seeing this apple here.
A general idea that can apply to many things, such as “apple” or “red.”
The mind’s ability to actively organize and connect what it receives.
A conscious mental representation that relates us to an object. Kant sometimes uses this word in a narrower, more technical way.
Putting different mental representations together so they form an organized whole.

questions_to_think_about: Can you notice something before you name or classify it?
Does recognizing an object require a general idea?
Could an animal have a direct awareness without using human-like concepts?
Why might it matter whether seeing something is merely caused by the world or can also support a belief?

summaries.example: Suppose you look at a tree and judge, “The tree is wet.” A Sensibilist interpretation may hold that a singular, immediate intuition of this particular tree can arise through sensibility without being built by concepts, while later judgment uses concepts to classify and describe it. An Intellectualist interpretation holds that the generation or organization of intuition already depends on some intellectual capacity, perhaps the power of apperception—the unity of consciousness—even if it does not require an explicit verbal judgment. Both views must explain how perception can concern an object, how error and hallucination are possible, and how experience can contribute to knowledge.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys the debate over the relation between Kant’s sensibility and intellect, especially the relation between intuition and concept. Kant characterizes intuition as immediate and particular, while concepts are general and mediate. Since cognition, in its narrower sense, requires cooperation between sensible intuition and intellectual activity, interpreters ask where intellectual contribution begins. The familiar Conceptualist position says that intuition has conceptual content; Nonconceptualism says that its content is at least partly nonconceptual. Yet the entry argues that this dispute may be poorly framed if “content” is understood in a contemporary, truth-condition-based way. Kant often treats content as a relation to an object, and he distinguishes the immediate relation of intuition from the mediated relation of concepts. A more flexible framework therefore contrasts Intellectualism and Sensibilism. Intellectualism holds that intuition depends on the intellect, perhaps through apperception, conceptual capacities, or judgment. Sensibilism holds that at least some intuitions can be generated independently of the intellect, while still allowing intellectual activity to be essential for perception, experience, judgment, or knowledge. The major disagreements concern whether intuition can justify belief, whether animals have conscious representations, how to understand the “blindness” of intuition, whether mathematical intuition is independent, and how Kant’s Transcendental Deduction and account of space and time should be interpreted. The entry does not present a settled resolution.
key_ideas: Kant distinguishes receptive sensibility from spontaneous intellectual activity, and assigns them different representational roles.
The traditional dispute is framed as Conceptualism versus Nonconceptualism: whether the content of intuition is conceptual or at least partly nonconceptual.
The entry argues that this content-based framing may impose a modern notion of representational content that does not fit Kant’s own account of content as a relation to an object.
A second framework asks about dependence: Intellectualism says intuition is at least partly dependent on the intellect, while Sensibilism allows that some intuitions arise independently of it.

The distinction between intuition, perception, and experience matters. Experience, in Kant’s technical sense, involves connected perceptions and conceptual synthesis; perception and intuition are more difficult cases.
The disagreement bears on justification, animal consciousness, mathematical construction, imagination, the unity of space and time, and the interpretation of the Transcendental Deduction.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate concerns a basic question about human cognition: how can a mind that receives sensory information also make judgments that are about an objective world and can be true or false? It also clarifies the difference between a causal effect on the senses and a contribution that can support knowledge. Because the arguments affect perception, rationality, animal minds, mathematics, and Kant’s theory of experience, the issue is important both historically and for contemporary philosophy of mind and epistemology.

important_terms.definition: A direct, immediate representation of a particular object; Kant contrasts it with the general and mediated representation supplied by a concept.
A general rule or representation through which different representations can be ordered under a common heading, normally in judgment.
The faculty of receiving representations when the mind is affected, contrasted with the intellect’s spontaneous activity.
A broad term for the higher cognitive capacities, including understanding, judgment, and reason.
The mind’s active combining of representations. Kant distinguishes intellectual synthesis from figurative synthesis carried out by imagination on sensible material.
Self-conscious unity of representations; the entry considers whether intuition depends on this power or on capacities that arise from it.

In Kant’s technical sense, cognition involving a conscious relation to an object; in its narrower sense it involves the cooperation of intuition and concepts and must concern a really possible subject matter.
The view that at least some intuitions are generated independently of the intellect and its intellectual acts.

questions_to_think_about: Does a sensory state need propositional or conceptual structure in order to justify a belief?
Can a representation be directed toward an object without having the kind of truth-evaluable content possessed by a judgment?
If animals lack an intellect, can they nevertheless have conscious intuitions?
Would making pure space and time depend on intellectual synthesis make Kant’s argument for the categories clearer, or would it make the argument circular or trivial?

What should “blind” mean in Kant’s claim that intuitions without concepts are blind: lack of object-awareness, lack of rational cognition, or difficulty in describing their contribution independently?

summaries.example: Think about looking at a bicycle. Your eyes receive a particular visual presentation: this bicycle, in this place, from this angle. You might then recognize it as a bicycle and judge that it is leaning against the wall. One interpretation says that the first presentation already depends on intellectual abilities that organize what you receive. Another says that the senses can provide a direct awareness first, while concepts and judgments help you understand and describe it later. The disagreement is not simply about whether thinking is useful; it is about what is required for the sensory representation itself.
summaries.summary: This entry examines a continuing dispute about how sensing and thinking cooperate in Kant’s philosophy. Kant divides the mind into different faculties. Sensibility is receptive: it is the capacity to be affected and to receive representations. The intellect is spontaneous: it actively combines and organizes representations. Kant describes intuition as immediate and particular, while a concept is general and relates to objects mediately. The central debate has often been called Conceptualism versus Nonconceptualism. Conceptualists maintain that intuition has conceptual content or that conceptual synthesis is required for its relation to an object. Nonconceptualists maintain that intuition has at least some nonconceptual contribution that can itself relate us to an object. The entry explains, however, that this framing may be misleading. Kant’s notion of content is not obviously the same as the modern idea of information with truth conditions. Also, Kant’s concepts normally function in judgments, so it is difficult to say exactly how they would provide the content of a merely sensory intuition. The entry therefore emphasizes a second framework: Intellectualism versus Sensibilism. Intellectualism says that the generation or structure of intuition depends on the intellect, perhaps through apperception or another intellectual activity. Sensibilism says that some intuitions, including possibly pure intuitions of space and time, can arise independently of the intellect. Both positions face challenges. Intellectualism must explain animal awareness and the distinctive contribution of sensibility. Sensibilism must explain how experience can support rational knowledge and how Kant’s argument for the categories works. The entry presents these as unresolved interpretive questions.
key_ideas: Kant separates two broad sides of mental activity: receptivity, through which the mind is affected, and spontaneity, through which it actively organizes representations.
Intuitions are immediate and particular; concepts are general and mediate. Kant treats both as important, but not identical, kinds of representation.

The original debate asks whether intuition has conceptual content. The entry suggests that this question may not match Kant’s own meaning of “content,” which is closely connected with a representation’s relation to an object.

A newer way to frame the disagreement asks whether intuition depends on the intellect. Intellectualists answer yes in some form; Sensibilists answer that at least some intuitions are independent of intellectual activity.
Kant’s technical meanings of intuition, perception, and experience are different. Experience is the most demanding of the three because it involves connected perceptions and conceptual synthesis.
The dispute affects questions about justification, animal awareness, imagination, geometry, the unity of space and time, and the Transcendental Deduction.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it concerns how perception can be about an objective world and how sense experience can connect with knowledge. It also helps distinguish a representation that merely happens because of a physical cause from one that can play a role in reasoning. Studying the disagreement shows why philosophical debates often depend not only on the proposed answers but also on how the question is framed.

important_terms.definition: A mind’s direct and particular representation of an object, rather than a general idea that applies to many objects.
A general representation or rule used to organize different representations under something common, usually through judgment.
The mind’s receptive capacity: its ability to be affected and receive sensory representations.
The mind’s active capacity to start organizing representations rather than merely receiving them.
Connecting or combining representations into an organized unity; Kant distinguishes kinds performed by the intellect and imagination.
A form of self-conscious unity through which representations can belong to one subject; some interpreters connect intuition’s dependence on the intellect to this power.
In Kant’s technical vocabulary, a conscious representation related to an object; in the narrower sense, cognition requires cooperation between intuition and concepts.
The position that at least some intuitions can be formed without dependence on the intellect itself.

questions_to_think_about: Can a sensory experience give someone a reason for a belief, or does it only cause the belief?
Is being aware of a particular object different from being able to describe or judge that object?
If animals do not have human intellectual faculties, what kinds of representations might they still have?
Why might the way we define “experience” change the answer to the conceptualism debate?
What does Kant’s phrase “intuitions without concepts are blind” seem to rule out, and what might it leave open?
